analysis.investment_thesis: India Glycols is a capital-intensive chemical manufacturer with a dangerously rising debt load (D/E 0.86, borrowings nearly doubling from ₹999 Cr to ₹2,055 Cr in 5 years) and four consecutive years of negative free cash flow. This is not a business I can own with confidence — the balance sheet disqualifies it before anything else.
key_strengths: Promoter holding stable at 59.63%, above my 55% floor
Operating income growing at 12.9% CAGR (faster than revenue), signalling some margin improvement
OCF positive all 5 of last 5 years, meaning core operations still generate cash
key_risks: D/E of 0.86 — nearly 3x my absolute ceiling of 0.3; borrowings surged from ₹1,047 Cr to ₹2,055 Cr in just 3 years
Capex-fuelled expansion (₹760 Cr in FY25 alone) is destroying FCF: -₹391 Cr in FY25, -₹103 Cr in FY24, no clear return timeline
ROE of 11.1% and ROCE of 12.4% — well below my 15-18% minimum; the business does not earn adequately on capital employed
red_flags: Borrowings nearly doubled in 3 years (₹1,047 Cr → ₹2,055 Cr) — classic aggressive debt-funded expansion
Free cash flow negative for 4 consecutive years: -264, -109, -103, -391 Cr — the company is not self-funding growth
Finance costs rising sharply from ₹70 Cr (FY22) to ₹164 Cr (FY25) — debt servicing is eating profits
FY22 net profit of ₹340 Cr was distorted by ₹260 Cr of other income — underlying earnings power is much weaker than it appears
analysis.detailed_analysis:
India Glycols fails my most fundamental test: a conservative balance sheet. A D/E of 0.86 is completely unacceptable in my framework, and the trend is worsening — borrowings have nearly doubled in three years while free cash flow has been negative every year since FY22. The company is clearly in an aggressive capex cycle (₹760 Cr capex in FY25 against ₹362 Cr OCF), funding expansion through debt rather than internal accruals. That is precisely the pattern that destroys shareholder value over a cycle when interest rates or business conditions turn.

The business itself is a complex, multi-segment chemicals operation — bio-based glycols, potable spirits, pharma ingredients, specialty gases — none of which fit my preference for simple, consumer-facing franchises with predictable demand. Revenue CAGR of only 5.5% over nine years barely keeps pace with inflation, and the ROE of 11.1% tells me management cannot earn adequately on the capital they deploy. At P/E of 24x, the market is pricing in a turnaround that the balance sheet cannot support. I would need to see D/E below 0.3, sustained positive FCF, and ROE above 15% before reconsidering.
